name: Ranka
tagline: Lingdum Monastery and green farm country, under an hour from Gangtok
meta_description: Ranka near Gangtok: Lingdum Monastery, Banjhakri Falls, village walks, how to get there and what it costs in 2026. An easy, low-cost half day out.
summary: Ranka is a rural area of farms and forest west of Gangtok, best known for Lingdum Monastery, a Zurmang Kagyu monastery completed in 1999. It makes an easy half-day trip, under an hour by car, and pairs well with Rumtek and Banjhakri Falls. Most visitors stay in Gangtok.
intro: Ranka lies on the hills west of Gangtok, a drive of under an hour through mixed forest, terraced fields and scattered houses. It is not a town so much as a spread of villages, and most people come for one reason: Lingdum Monastery, also called Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery. Completed in 1999, it is one of the newer large monasteries in Sikkim, with a wide stone courtyard and a richly painted main hall. The lower Lingdum area sits at about 1,300 m.

On the way out of Gangtok, many drivers stop at Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park, about 7 km from town. It is a landscaped park around a waterfall of roughly 30 m, with statues about the Ban Jhakri, the forest shaman of Nepali folk belief, and a small hall on renewable energy. Families like it. If you prefer quiet, skip it and spend the time at the monastery or walking the farm lanes instead.

Ranka is a good choice if you have one free half-day in Gangtok and want something calmer than the viewpoint circuit. A reserved car costs about ₹1,500–2,500 for the return trip, indicative for 2026, or ₹2,000–3,000 if you add Rumtek. There are no big hotels here and we do not list any stays; sleep in Gangtok. Carry water and snacks, as food options near the monastery are limited. Bring a warm layer outside summer.

story.title: A Kham lineage on a Sikkim hillside
paras: Lingdum Monastery belongs to the Zurmang Kagyu tradition, a branch of the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism. The lineage takes its name from the Zurmang monasteries in Kham, in eastern Tibet, where it grew over several centuries. Like many Tibetan lineages after 1959, it rebuilt part of its life in exile. Lingdum, completed in 1999 near Ranka, became its main centre in Sikkim, led by Zurmang Gharwang Rinpoche. The site faces the hills west of Gangtok.

That makes Lingdum very young by Sikkim standards. Rumtek's first monastery dates to the mid-18th century, and Enchey's present building to 1909. Yet Lingdum follows the old forms: a large courtyard of the kind used for ritual dances, a main hall with painted pillars and murals, and young monks in training. Visitors see a working monastery in full use, not a museum, which is part of its appeal. Rituals here run to the Tibetan lunar calendar.

Ranka's other well-known stop has a folk story behind it. In Nepali tradition, the Ban Jhakri is a forest shaman, a healer said to live among caves and trees. Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park, on the road towards Ranka, was planned after Chief Minister Pawan Kumar Chamling visited the waterfall on 28 September 2004, on his way back from Ranka Monastery. Statues in the park retell the shaman tradition, which belongs to folklore rather than recorded history.
story.source: Wikipedia articles Lingdum Monastery and Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park; Wikipedia articles Karma Kagyu and Rumtek Monastery for comparison dates

did_you_know: Lingdum Monastery, also called Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery, was completed in 1999.
In Nepali, ban means forest and jhakri means healer, so the Ban Jhakri of Banjhakri Falls is a forest shaman in folk belief.
Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park was planned after the Chief Minister visited the waterfall on 28 September 2004, returning from Ranka Monastery.
facts: Lingdum Monastery, Banjhakri Falls, farm villages

highlights.title: Lingdum Monastery courtyard
highlights.text: Lingdum's wide courtyard is lined with monastery buildings, with the main hall at the head of a flight of steps. It is spacious, clean and usually calm. Come in the morning or late afternoon, when monks gather for prayers and the light is soft on the painted front.

highlights.title: The main prayer hall
highlights.text: Inside, the main hall has painted pillars, wall murals and large images on the altar. If you arrive during prayers, sit quietly at the back. Take off your shoes, keep your voice low, do not use flash, and ask before photographing anyone. Leave a small offering if you wish.

highlights.title: Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park
highlights.text: About 7 km from Gangtok on the way towards Ranka, this landscaped park surrounds a waterfall of roughly 30 m. Statues tell the story of the Ban Jhakri, the forest shaman of Nepali folk belief, and a hall shows renewable energy. Entry is a small fee, about ₹20–100, indicative.

highlights.title: Farm lanes around Ranka
highlights.text: Ranka is farm country, with terraced fields of crops such as maize, ginger and vegetables, and cows tethered by the houses. Walk a lane below the monastery for half an hour and you will see daily village life. Sikkim is a fully organic state, so farmers here do not use chemical fertilisers.

highlights.title: Rumtek on the same day
highlights.text: Rumtek, the Karmapa's seat in exile, is close enough to combine with Ranka in a single day. One reserved car covering both costs about ₹2,000–3,000, indicative for 2026. Go to Rumtek first for morning prayers, then come to Lingdum when it is quieter in the afternoon.

how_to_reach.text: Shared taxis towards Ranka run from Gangtok, mainly for locals, at about ₹50–100 a seat, indicative 2026. They are less frequent than Rumtek taxis and may drop you a walk from the monastery. Ask at your hotel which stand they use that season, and check the time of the last one back.

A reserved car from Gangtok to Lingdum and back costs about ₹1,500–2,500 with waiting time, or ₹2,000–3,000 if you add Rumtek, indicative for 2026. The drive takes under an hour each way. Many Gangtok half-day sightseeing packages also include Ranka and Banjhakri Falls.

Come via Gangtok. The nearest airport is Bagdogra (IXB) and the nearest big railway station is NJP, both four to five hours away by road. Pakyong Airport has no scheduled flights as of 2026, and there is no railway in Sikkim yet. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: We suggest staying in Gangtok and visiting Ranka on a half-day trip, as there are no well-known hotels in Ranka itself. Budget travellers can use Tibet Road or MG Marg guest houses and take a shared taxi out. Comfort travellers might base themselves on the western side of Gangtok to shorten the drive. If you want a night outside the city, Bamboo Retreat near Rumtek is a comfortable choice within easy reach of Lingdum. Some village families around Ranka take homestay guests informally; ask a registered Gangtok agent rather than booking unverified listings online.
costs: Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park entry
budget_tip: Ask your driver to fold Ranka into a Rumtek half-day for one car fare of about ₹2,000–3,000, rather than booking two separate trips from Gangtok.
tips: Dress modestly at Lingdum, with shoulders and knees covered, and remove shoes before entering the prayer hall.
Carry water and a snack, as there are few cafés near the monastery and you may wait a while for prayers.
Agree the stops and waiting time with your driver before you set off, so Banjhakri Falls and Rumtek are not charged as extras later.
In the monsoon, clouds and rain often hide the valley views, so save Ranka for a dry morning if you have the choice.
Entry fees at Banjhakri Falls and the monasteries can change, so check current status before you travel and carry small notes.

experiences.title: Morning prayers at Lingdum Monastery
experiences.summary: An early drive from Gangtok to Lingdum, the Zurmang Kagyu monastery completed in 1999, to hear the monks' morning prayers and walk the wide courtyard before visitors arrive. Calm, low-cost and easy for all ages.
body: Leave Gangtok around 7 am in a reserved car. The road winds west through forest and farmland, and you reach Lingdum in under an hour. From the parking area, a short walk brings you into the courtyard. It is a large, open square, with buildings along the sides and the main hall at the top of a flight of steps. In the early morning it is usually almost empty. Mist often hangs in the valley at this hour.

If prayers are on, you will hear them before you reach the hall: long horns, drums, cymbals and the low chant of many voices. Take off your shoes, step inside quietly and sit at the back on the floor or a bench. Do not walk in front of seated monks, and never use flash. Stay as long as you like; nobody minds a respectful visitor who sits still. Prayers can last an hour or more.

Afterwards, walk around the hall clockwise and look at the painted pillars and wall murals. Young novices may be heading to class with their books. There is usually no fixed entry fee, but a small donation is welcome. Prayer times shift with the ritual calendar, so ask your hotel the evening before. Back in the car by about 10 am, you can still add Rumtek or Banjhakri Falls on the way home.

faqs.q: How far is Lingdum Monastery from Gangtok
faqs.a: Lingdum Monastery at Ranka is roughly 15–20 km from Gangtok, depending on the road taken, and the drive takes under an hour. A reserved car for the return trip with waiting time costs about ₹1,500–2,500, indicative for 2026. Shared taxis towards Ranka exist but are less frequent and may leave you with a walk.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Lingdum and Ranka Monastery
faqs.a: There is none. Lingdum Monastery, Ranka Monastery and Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery are names for the same place. It follows the Zurmang Kagyu tradition and was completed in 1999. Drivers in Gangtok often just call it Ranka Monastery, so use that name when you book a car if Lingdum gets a blank look.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Lingdum Monastery
faqs.a: Photos of the courtyard and the outside of the main hall are generally fine. Inside the hall, rules can vary, so look for signs or ask a monk first. Never use flash during prayers, and do not photograph monks closely without permission. Novices are often shy, so a smile and a question go a long way.

experiences.title: Banjhakri Falls and the shaman story
experiences.summary: A short stop on the road towards Ranka at a landscaped park around a waterfall of about 30 m. Statues tell the Ban Jhakri forest shaman tradition, and a small hall covers renewable energy. Easy, family-friendly and cheap.
body: Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park lies about 7 km from Gangtok on the way towards Ranka. It was planned after Chief Minister Pawan Kumar Chamling visited the falls in September 2004, returning from Ranka Monastery. Today it is a landscaped park with paved footpaths and viewing spots around a waterfall of roughly 30 m. Paths are paved and gentle, so it suits families with small children and older travellers. Allow an hour for a relaxed visit.

The name comes from Nepali folk belief. Ban means forest and jhakri means healer, so the Ban Jhakri is a forest shaman, said in tradition to live among caves and trees and to teach healing to those he chooses. Statues around the park depict the Ban Jhakri and shaman rituals. Treat them as folklore, told in a public park, not as a full account of living shaman practice in Sikkim.

There is also a museum hall on renewable energy, with displays on solar water heaters and other equipment, and the park is lit by solar-powered lamps. Entry is a small fee, roughly ₹20–100, indicative for 2026, with extra charges possible for cameras or parking. Weekends and school holidays get crowded. The fall is fullest from July to September, but September and October give a good flow with safer roads. Carry a light rain jacket for the spray.

faqs.q: How much is the entry fee at Banjhakri Falls
faqs.a: Entry to Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park is a small fee, reported at roughly ₹20–100 per person, indicative for 2026, and there may be extra charges for cameras or parking. Fees change, so check current status before you travel and carry small notes. Many Gangtok sightseeing packages include the stop but not the ticket.

faqs.q: What is a Ban Jhakri
faqs.a: In Nepali folk belief, the Ban Jhakri is a forest shaman. Ban means forest and jhakri means healer. Tradition holds that he lives among caves and trees and may take a chosen person away to teach them healing. The park near Gangtok uses statues to tell these stories. It is folklore, so treat the details as tradition, not history.

faqs.q: Is Banjhakri Falls worth visiting
faqs.a: It is worth an hour if you are travelling with children or older relatives, or if you want an easy stop on the way to Ranka. The park is tidy, paths are gentle and the waterfall is pleasant after rain. If you prefer wild places, skip it and spend the time at Lingdum Monastery or on a village walk instead.

experiences.title: Farm lanes and organic fields at Ranka
experiences.summary: A gentle walk on the lanes below Lingdum through terraced fields, kitchen gardens and small homes. Sikkim is a fully organic state, and Ranka is a good place to see what that looks like on small farms. Free, easy and best in the morning.
body: After visiting Lingdum, ask your driver to wait and walk down one of the lanes below the monastery for half an hour or an hour. You are likely to pass terraces of maize and vegetables, patches of ginger, and in shaded spots the broad leaves of large cardamom, one of Sikkim's main cash crops. Houses sit among their own gardens, with chickens, cows and stacks of firewood. Give way to anyone carrying loads on narrow paths.

Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in January 2016, after phasing out chemical fertilisers and pesticides. On farms like these, that means compost, cow manure and mixed planting. Farmers are busy people, so greet them, but do not walk into fields or private yards without being invited. If someone offers tea, accept it gracefully and do not offer money unless it is clearly a shop. Ask before photographing people or homes.

The walk is free and needs no guide, though a local driver can point out the right lanes. Wear shoes with grip, as paths are often wet. Carry your own water and bring your rubbish back to Gangtok. The best light and the most activity are in the morning. From June to September leeches can be common on grassy paths, so keep to the road and check your socks afterwards.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for a village walk at Ranka
faqs.a: No. The lanes around Ranka are open public roads and paths, and you can walk them on your own. Your driver can suggest a loop and wait for you. If you want to learn more about farming or local life, ask a Gangtok agent to arrange a local host, and agree any fee in advance.

faqs.q: What does organic farming in Sikkim mean
faqs.a: Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in January 2016. The state phased out chemical fertilisers and pesticides, so farmers use compost, manure and natural pest control. For visitors, it means the vegetables, ginger and cardamom you see on Ranka's terraces are grown without synthetic chemicals. Local markets in Gangtok sell this produce.

faqs.q: Are there leeches at Ranka
faqs.a: Yes, in the wet months. From June to September, leeches are common on grassy and forest paths across Sikkim, including around Ranka. They are harmless but unpleasant. Keep to roads and paved lanes, wear long socks over your trousers, and check your feet afterwards. From October to May they are rarely a problem.

experiences.title: Ranka and Rumtek monastery loop
experiences.summary: One car, two great monasteries: Rumtek, seat in exile of the Karmapa, and Lingdum at Ranka, completed in 1999. A full morning to early afternoon from Gangtok, good value when shared by three or four people.
body: This loop suits travellers with one free day in Gangtok who want monasteries rather than viewpoints. Start early and go to Rumtek first, about an hour from town. Spend two hours there: the main hall of the Dharma Chakra Centre, the golden stupa with the 16th Karmapa's relics, and the courtyard facing the Karma Shri Nalanda Institute. Carry photo ID for the police check at the gate. Bags may be checked at the gate too.

Have tea in Rumtek village, then drive on to Ranka. Your driver will pick the road that is in best shape that season. At Lingdum, the courtyard is broad and calm, and the main hall is newer and brighter than Rumtek's. The contrast is part of the point: Rumtek carries the weight of 1960s exile history, while Lingdum shows a lineage building afresh in the late 1990s. Sit quietly at the back during prayers.

On the way back, stop at Banjhakri Falls if you have children with you, or skip it to save time. A reserved car for the whole loop costs about ₹2,000–3,000, indicative for 2026, so it is cheap when shared. Dress modestly for both monasteries and carry small notes for offerings. In the monsoon, roads can be slow and views cloudy, so check current status before you travel. Be back in Gangtok by mid-afternoon.

faqs.q: Should I visit Rumtek or Ranka first
faqs.a: Go to Rumtek first. It is the bigger draw, gets more tour cars as the day goes on, and its morning prayers are worth hearing. Lingdum at Ranka stays calmer into the afternoon. Doing it in this order also lets you finish at Banjhakri Falls on the way back to Gangtok if you want an easy last stop.

faqs.q: How much does a Rumtek and Ranka car cost
faqs.a: A reserved car from Gangtok covering Rumtek and Lingdum at Ranka costs about ₹2,000–3,000, indicative for 2026, depending on season, vehicle size and extra stops. Agree the stops and waiting time before you start. Shared between four people, that is roughly ₹500–750 each, cheaper than two separate trips.

faqs.q: Is this loop suitable for elderly travellers
faqs.a: Mostly, yes. Both monasteries have steps up to the main halls, but there is little other walking, and the car can park close by. Take the steps slowly and use handrails where they exist. The drive is winding, so anyone prone to car sickness should sit in front and take medicine beforehand.

faqs.q: Is Ranka worth visiting from Gangtok
faqs.a: Yes, if you have a free half-day and like quiet places. Lingdum Monastery at Ranka is large, open and calm, with a courtyard that sees fewer crowds than Rumtek. The drive is under an hour through farmland and forest. Combined with Rumtek or Banjhakri Falls, it makes a good-value day out from Gangtok.

faqs.q: What is Ranka famous for
faqs.a: Ranka is best known for Lingdum Monastery, also called Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery or simply Ranka Monastery, completed in 1999 in the Zurmang Kagyu tradition. On the way from Gangtok is Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park. The rest of Ranka is quiet farm country with terraced fields and small villages.

faqs.q: How do I get to Ranka from Gangtok
faqs.a: The easiest way is a reserved car, about ₹1,500–2,500 for the return trip with waiting time, indicative for 2026. The drive takes under an hour. Shared taxis towards Ranka exist, at about ₹50–100 a seat, but they run less often and may not stop at the monastery gate. Many half-day sightseeing packages include Ranka.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Ranka
faqs.a: There are no well-known hotels in Ranka, and we do not list any. A few village families may host guests, but check carefully through a registered Gangtok agent. Most travellers stay in Gangtok and visit on a half-day trip. If you want a night out of the city nearby, Bamboo Retreat near Rumtek is a comfortable option.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Ranka
faqs.a: March to May and October to December are best, with dry roads and clearer valley views. Spring brings flowers to the farm lanes; autumn has the sharpest light. Winter mornings are cold but often clear. From June to September, rain, leeches and occasional landslides make the drive slower, though the monastery stays open.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Lingdum Monastery
faqs.a: Lingdum Monastery has usually been free to enter, or charged only a small fee of up to about ₹50, indicative for 2026. A donation in the offering box is welcome but not required. Fees can change, so check current status before you travel and carry small notes. Banjhakri Falls, on the way, charges its own small entry fee.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Ranka
faqs.a: Allow two to three hours at Ranka, including time in the prayer hall and courtyard, plus up to an hour each way from Gangtok. Add an hour for Banjhakri Falls, or two to three hours for Rumtek if you do the full loop. A half-day is enough for Ranka alone; a full day covers all three comfortably.

faqs.q: Is Ranka good for families with children
faqs.a: Yes. The drive is short, the monastery courtyard is safe and open, and Banjhakri Falls and Energy Park on the way has gentle paths, statues and a waterfall that children enjoy. Teach children to stay quiet in the prayer hall and not to touch altars. Carry snacks, as food options near Lingdum are limited.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Ranka and Lingdum
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign nationals with a valid Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, also called an Inner Line Permit, can visit Ranka and Lingdum Monastery without any extra permit. Carry your passport and permit in case of checks. The permit is free and issued online, at Rangpo and at Sikkim Tourism offices. Check current status before you travel.
